cases.abstract: Personalizing a text-to-image model must retain a particular subject without reducing generation to its few reference views. DreamBooth fine-tunes pretrained diffusion models on three to five images, pairing a rare-token identifier with a class descriptor so the learned instance can draw on the model's class knowledge. To prevent that class from collapsing into the instance, a prior-preservation loss rehearses class images generated by the frozen model. We implement this approach with Imagen and Stable Diffusion and release a 30-subject dataset and evaluation protocol, proposing DINO similarity to measure subject distinctions that text-aligned image embeddings may overlook. Across 3,000 generated images, Stable Diffusion DreamBooth increases DINO similarity from 0.569 to 0.668 and CLIP prompt alignment from 0.255 to 0.305 over Textual Inversion, supporting subject retention together with prompt responsiveness. Users likewise prefer DreamBooth for subject fidelity (68% versus 22%) and prompt fidelity (81% versus 12%). An Imagen ablation shows that prior preservation reduces class collapse and increases diversity while slightly lowering subject fidelity. Examples include new contexts, viewpoints, artistic renditions, and property changes; rare contexts, appearance entanglement, overfitting, and hallucinated details limit these capabilities.
cases.notes: Revised around learning an instance while retaining usable class knowledge, rather than enumerating personalization components. Section 3.2 grounds the identifier/class relationship; Section 3.3 grounds class-image supervision. Tables 1-2 jointly answer identity and prompt fidelity on Stable Diffusion, not whether each design choice caused the gain. Table 3 bounds prior preservation as a diversity/class-retention tradeoff. Kept the public dataset/protocol and DINO metric as co-contributions, with qualitative applications and Section 4.5 failures scoped accordingly.

cases.abstract: Toolformer learns when and how to invoke external APIs from feedback on whether their responses improve continuation prediction. A few demonstrations per text-based API guide candidate calls; executed calls survive only if their results lower next-token loss relative to both no call and a call without its result. Fine-tuning GPT-J on these augmented texts turns predictive utility into supervision for tool selection and use, without downstream-task demonstrations. In prompted zero-shot evaluations permitting at most one call with call-encouraging decoding, Toolformer improves factual completion, arithmetic, question answering, and temporal tasks over GPT-J baselines. On ASDiv, first-number accuracy is 40.4% with calls enabled versus 14.8% with calls disabled, indicating that inference-time access adds benefit beyond tool-annotated training. We introduce the template-generated DATESET benchmark, where calendar access supplies useful temporal context. Search-assisted question answering remains below GPT-3; translation helps the tool-trained model across languages but does not consistently beat original GPT-J. With calls disabled, perplexity matches content-matched fine-tuning without API annotations. In three-tool scaling tests, most benefits emerge around 775M parameters, with search an exception. Independently generated training calls do not teach chained or interactive tool use.
cases.notes: Revised to connect predictive-utility filtering to learned tool decisions, then use the same model with calls enabled versus disabled to distinguish inference-time tool benefit from annotation training alone (Section 2; Table 3). The result is scoped to first-number scoring, including its equation exception, and prompted zero-shot evaluation with one call maximum and top-10 API-marker triggering. Retained DATESET, mixed QA/translation findings, content-matched perplexity, and three-tool scaling with the search exception. Independent call generation explains the absence of chained training, not a general limit on language models.
